thesis: Held position, and the 60-day signal is a +31.8% advance with a company-disclosed cause: fiscal Q4 2026 (reported 29 July 2026) revenue rose 18% to $90B and EPS rose 30% to $4.74 against a $4.24 consensus, Microsoft Cloud revenue rose 27% to $59.3B, Azure grew 43% against roughly 40.4% expected and passed a $100B annual revenue scale, and management guided fiscal Q1 to 45% Azure growth at constant currency, above consensus. The strongest counter-evidence is this week's AI-infrastructure de-rating: a WSJ report that Anthropic's $65B ARR fell short of $80B-plus whisper figures triggered risk-off selling across AI hardware on 18 August, alongside a 30-year Treasury yield above 5.3%, and MSFT itself has given back roughly 4% from its 10 August close. That does not change the read, because the repricing is driven by a third-party revenue datapoint and a rate move rather than by any change in Microsoft's own disclosure — the 45% constant-currency Azure guide was issued on 29 July and has not been revised, and it sits on a cloud base of $59.3B a quarter rather than on any single AI lab's spending. A securities class action over Copilot-related statements is pending in the Western District of Washington (lead-plaintiff deadline was 11 August 2026); no scheduled ruling, hearing or trial date was found in this run's research, so it is noted here rather than flagged.
invalidation: Microsoft revises the Azure constant-currency growth guide below the mid-30s, or reports Azure growth materially under the guided 45%, at its next quarterly report

thesis: Held position with no Step 2 signal this run (60-day move 4.5%, volume 1.13x), so this is the mandatory fresh read rather than a reaction to a move. The company-disclosed basis is fiscal Q1 2027, reported 28 May 2026: revenue up 88%, AI-optimised server revenue up 757% to $16.1B, AI server backlog of $51.3B, and full-year fiscal 2027 revenue guidance raised to $165-169B including roughly $60B of AI servers. The strongest counter-evidence is the AI-hardware de-rating now under way — the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 4.98% on 18 August as the 30-year Treasury yield passed 5.3% — against a stock that has roughly tripled year to date and so carries obvious positioning risk. That argues for caution on adding rather than on holding, because the backlog and the raised guidance are company-issued figures that have not been revised by the week's move. Conviction is capped at medium rather than high by an unresolved binary event inside the holding window: Dell's fiscal Q2 2027 report is expected on 1 September 2026, roughly two weeks out, and either the AI-server margin profile or the backlog conversion rate disclosed there could reverse this read. No lawsuit or regulatory proceeding naming Dell with a scheduled next step in the coming ~90 days surfaced in this run's research.
invalidation: the 1 September fiscal Q2 report shows AI server backlog declining sequentially, or full-year guidance is cut from the $165-169B range

thesis: Held position. Company-disclosed results are strong: fiscal Q4 2026, reported 12 August 2026, came in at $2.05B revenue and $1.74 adjusted EPS against a $1.58 estimate, a seventh consecutive record-revenue quarter, with fiscal Q1 guidance of $1.85-2.05 EPS against $1.77 consensus, and the stock rose about 9% on the print. The tape since then says the opposite by a wide margin — down roughly 21% from the 17 August close, and 32.4% over the 60-day window — so the disclosed beat alone does not explain it, and further research was run before writing this. What that turned up is a sector-wide repricing rather than anything company-specific: Fabrinet fell about 20% on 18 August despite record Q4 revenue of $1.316B (up 45% year over year), Applied Optoelectronics and Corning fell double digits the same day, and the trigger cited was a WSJ report that Anthropic's $65B ARR missed $80B-plus whisper figures, on a day when the 30-year Treasury yield passed 5.3%. Coherent was reported trading at a trailing P/E near 160x into that reset. This still supports holding, because the disclosed order book and above-consensus guidance are intact, but the decline is a valuation and sentiment unwind rather than a disclosed fundamental deterioration, which caps conviction at low. No lawsuit or regulatory proceeding naming Coherent with a scheduled next step in the coming ~90 days surfaced in this run's research.
invalidation: Coherent cuts or walks back the $1.85-2.05 fiscal Q1 EPS guide, or discloses order cancellations or push-outs in its AI datacenter transceiver business

thesis: Held position, flagged on a 34.3% 60-day decline. The company-disclosed results run the other way: Q2 2026, reported 4 August 2026, showed record revenue of $392.4M, up 104% year over year on PCIe 6 demand, with fiscal Q3 guidance of $540-560M, roughly 40% sequential growth at the midpoint and above what analysts expected. The reported explanation for the roughly 12% drop since that print is profit-taking after a large run rather than a disclosed miss, compounded by the broad AI-hardware de-rating of 18 August; that framing is what caps this at low, because it treats the move as positioning rather than as evidence about the business. Two genuine negatives were found and neither is settled: Q2 operating expenses rose on continued product-roadmap investment, and Broadcom, the incumbent in datacenter PCIe switching, is reported to have accelerated its own PCIe switch roadmap in response to Astera's rise — a competitive threat this run's research cannot size. Astera is still up sharply year to date and the Q3 guide postdates the competitive dynamic, which is why this reads as continuing to support holding rather than as a reason to exit. No lawsuit or regulatory proceeding naming Astera Labs with a scheduled next step in the coming ~90 days surfaced in this run's research.
invalidation: Astera guides fiscal Q4 below the fiscal Q3 revenue range, or discloses share loss at a major hyperscaler customer to a competing PCIe switch supplier

thesis: Flagged on both a 49.3% 60-day advance and a close 2.6% from its 52-week high — the only candidate this run tripping two criteria. The catalyst is confirmed and company-disclosed: second-quarter fiscal 2026 record revenue of $256.1M, up 32% year over year, with 2026 revenue guidance raised to as much as $1.2B. Supporting disclosures are the Phase 3 ROSELLA data presented at ASCO, showing a 35% reduction in risk of death and median overall survival of 16.0 versus 11.9 months in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer, and the resubmission of the relacorilant New Drug Application for Cushing's syndrome on 17 June 2026. The strongest counter-evidence is that regulatory file: the FDA issued a complete response letter on 31 December 2025 declining the original application, and the resubmission carries an expected six-month review, putting an action date around late 2026. That is engaged rather than dismissed. It does not undercut the raised guidance itself, because relacorilant is not approved in Cushing's and 2026 revenue guidance therefore cannot depend on it. What this run could not establish from any source it read is how much of the current price embeds an approval, so the guidance read is clean but the valuation read is not, which is why this is medium and not high. No lawsuit or regulatory proceeding naming Corcept with a scheduled next step in the coming ~90 days surfaced in this run's research.
invalidation: Corcept cuts the 2026 revenue guidance range, or the FDA issues a second complete response letter on the relacorilant Cushing's resubmission

thesis: Flagged on a 22.9% 60-day decline, but today's news runs the other way and is company-disclosed: a securities filing on 19 August 2026 discloses an expanded Google partnership under which Google may purchase up to $12.2B of Marvell shares — up to 58,970,907 shares at $206.58 — tied to procurement goals running through fiscal 2033, alongside custom silicon work attaching to Google's TPU ecosystem across AI inference accelerators, storage, network interface and memory interface controllers. Marvell separately launched AI memory infrastructure products the same day (Bravera SC6 SSD controller, Structera X CXL memory expansion, Photonic Fabric), with Bravera SC6 sampling expected in the fourth quarter, and the shares rose roughly 8-14% on the combination. The counter-evidence is embedded in the same filing rather than external to it: the share purchase right is a pending equity issuance of nearly 59 million shares, which is dilution against a strategic anchor rather than a free option, and it is priced at $206.58, below today's $238.63. This suggests an anchor-customer relationship rather than establishing one — the purchase right is contingent on procurement goals this run's research could not verify. The dilution_risk flag is present, which sets conviction at low regardless of how the strategic logic reads.
invalidation: the Google share purchase agreement is amended or terminated, or Marvell's next quarterly report shows custom-silicon revenue declining sequentially

thesis: Flagged on an 11.9% 60-day decline, the mildest drawdown of any candidate that qualified this run. The company-disclosed data point cuts against the price: TSMC's July 2026 monthly revenue rose 44.7% year over year to NT$467.58B, taking first-seven-month revenue to NT$2.87 trillion, up 37%, and management expects full-year 2026 revenue growth slightly above 40% in US dollar terms. The 4%-plus fall on 18 August is attributed to an indiscriminate semiconductor selloff on rising long-end Treasury yields rather than to anything in TSMC's own reporting. Naming the counter-case: that same macro driver is unresolved — if the 30-year yield above 5.3% reflects a durable repricing of AI infrastructure financing costs, then customer capex, not TSMC's execution, is what gets cut, and this run found nothing that settles that question either way. Because the proximate cause of the move is macro and sector-wide rather than company-specific, conviction is low by rubric regardless of how strong the July revenue print is.
invalidation: a monthly revenue report shows year-over-year growth decelerating below 20%, or management guides full-year 2026 US dollar revenue growth below 40%

thesis: Flagged on a 34.2% 60-day decline, the second-largest of this run. The proximate cause is company-disclosed and dilutive: Intel priced an upsized public equity offering of roughly 210.5 million shares at $95, lifting the raise to about $20B from $15B, one of the largest equity raises in semiconductor history, and the shares fell on the dilution. UBS then cut its price target to $112 from $121 while keeping a Neutral rating. Set against that, Bank of America's Vivek Arya reads the same raise as a signal of management confidence in internal foundry demand and external customer interest — a real counter-case, and one this run cannot settle, since nothing read here discloses committed external foundry volume. Broader factors are also in the mix: an ongoing Iran conflict weighing on capital-intensive growth names and competitive pressure in advanced manufacturing. Multiple contributing factors with none clearly dominant, plus a completed raise diluting existing holders and an unsettled foundry question, is not a setup this pipeline should enter on.
invalidation: Intel discloses a named external foundry customer committing volume at 18A or 14A, which would convert the raise from dilution into funded demand

thesis: Flagged on a 31.0% 60-day decline. This run found no company-specific negative disclosure behind it. The reported explanation is a memory-complex unwind: SanDisk fell about 6% to $1,681.10 on 18 August as rising Treasury yields pressured what is described as the most extended trade in the semiconductor sector, with Micron down 5% and Western Digital down 7% the same session, and the move is characterised as momentum unwinding rather than a fresh company-specific headline. The stock is still up nearly 600% year to date and roughly 30% off its peak. The one company-level datapoint that is not flattering is relative: TrendForce reports strong Q2 2026 AI server demand and rising NAND average selling prices, but SanDisk's 50.7% quarterly growth lagged the top five memory makers. So the decline is sentiment- and rate-driven while the operating datapoint is mildly negative on a relative basis, and neither resolves the other. That is unresolved evidence around a name that has already run 600% this year, not an entry.
invalidation: SanDisk's next quarterly report shows NAND revenue growth back in line with or ahead of the memory peer group, with the sector-wide rate pressure abating

thesis: Flagged on a 28.6% 60-day decline. Applied Optoelectronics' Q2 2026 report of 6 August publishes metrics pointing in opposite directions and both belong here: revenue of $191.9M was up 86% year over year and 27% sequentially against roughly $190M expected, a fifth consecutive record quarter, and non-GAAP EPS of $0.06 beat a $0.01 estimate on a return to non-GAAP profitability — but the Q3 guide of $0.11-0.26 non-GAAP EPS sits below the $0.28 consensus, and the $255-290M revenue guide straddles the $278M estimate rather than clearing it. Data center revenue was $107.7M and CATV $80.6M, with 800G revenue more than doubling sequentially. The price then fell 17-21% on 18-19 August as the whole photonics complex reset — Fabrinet down about 20% despite a record Q4, Coherent and Lumentum down double digits, triggered by a WSJ report on Anthropic's $65B ARR undershooting whisper figures. So there is a genuine revenue beat, a soft earnings guide, and a sector-wide sentiment unwind layered on top, none of which this run can rank as dominant.
invalidation: AAOI delivers Q3 non-GAAP EPS at or above the $0.28 consensus while holding data center revenue growth, which would settle the guidance question against the beat

thesis: Flagged on a 27.3% 60-day decline with two distinct causes, neither of which cancels the other. Company-specific first: Corning's Q2 2026 report on 28 July beat on both revenue and earnings, but Q3 guidance of $4.9-5.0B revenue and $0.85-0.89 EPS came in slightly below elevated consensus and the stock fell more than 20% in a single session. Within that report the key AI-linked segment, Optical Communications, grew 32% year over year to $2.07B — strong in absolute terms, but decelerating from 36% the prior quarter, and that deceleration is what the reaction focused on. Corning reaffirmed its Springboard plan targeting a $20B annualised sales run rate, and says it expects to hit that run rate in Q3, a quarter ahead of schedule. Layered on top, Corning fell about 8.2% on 18 August in the sector-wide optics repricing tied to the WSJ report on Anthropic's ARR. A beat paired with a soft guide, an accelerating run-rate target paired with a decelerating growth segment, and a macro unwind on top — the evidence is offsetting and this run cannot resolve which reading dominates.
invalidation: Corning delivers the $20B annualised run rate in Q3 with Optical Communications growth re-accelerating above the prior 36% rate, which would settle the deceleration question

thesis: Flagged on a 24.4% 60-day decline. The cause is company-disclosed but not yet a confirmed event: on the Q2 earnings call CEO Peter Beck said production still lines up with delivering Neutron to the pad in Q4 2026 while declining to reaffirm a first flight before year end, saying the window for an end-of-year launch is narrowing and that the work now is risk trading against how quickly the company can scale to a tenth launch. Shares fell more than 9% premarket on the possibility the debut slips to 2027. The counter-case is real and quantified: Q2 revenue of $234.07M was up 62% year over year, the company signed $437M of new launch contracts, and backlog reached a record $2.36B. It does not offset the timeline risk, because Neutron is the medium-lift growth thesis and record Electron-era revenue and backlog do not substitute for it — a slip pushes the entire revenue step-change a year right. Conviction stops at medium rather than going higher because the slip itself is not confirmed: management has neither reaffirmed nor withdrawn the year-end target, so the adverse catalyst is still pending.
invalidation: Rocket Lab confirms a Neutron first flight date before the end of 2026, or completes the stage-one delivery to the pad on the stated Q4 schedule

thesis: Flagged on a 22.6% 60-day decline. Nothing found in this run's research points to a company-specific cause. Micron briefly reclaimed $1,000 before falling about 7% to roughly $940 on 18 August, and the reported drivers are macro: the 30-year Treasury yield surged past 5.3% to a multi-year high with the 10-year near 4.75%, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 4.98% the same session, and the selloff is explicitly described as sector-wide rather than company-specific. Against that, the underlying memory market is reported as remaining tight with much of Micron's 2027 capacity already allocated, and the stock is still up nearly 240% year to date. The counter-case therefore is that this is an entry point into an intact cycle; what this run cannot settle is whether higher financing costs for AI infrastructure eventually reduce the customer capex that tightness rests on. A macro-driven drawdown in a name that has already tripled this year, with the demand question open, is not an entry for this account.
invalidation: long-end Treasury yields retrace and Micron's next quarterly report confirms 2027 capacity remains allocated at rising contract prices

thesis: Flagged on both a 21.1% 60-day decline and a 2.05x volume spike — the only candidate this run tripping the volume criterion. The company-disclosed results are genuinely strong: Q2 2026 revenue grew 454% year over year with the AI Cloud segment up 514%, the company reports over $40B in customer commitments and four landmark deals averaging more than $1B in total contract value each, and the shares rose 34% on the print. What the volume spike is measuring, though, is not that print. Nebius is described as whipsawing on meme-driven trading, lighting up WallStreetBets feeds on 19 August, with back-to-back sessions spiking 27.1% and 9.3% and no fundamental catalyst cited for them, and the stock fell roughly 17% over the last three sessions after gaining 34%. So the flagged signal is mechanical and flow-driven rather than a read on the business, which discounts its fundamental significance. The disclosed growth is a strong counter-case to avoiding this and it is not resolved here — but a position entered into meme-flow volatility on a pipeline that reviews stops once a day, with no resting stop at the broker, is the wrong risk to take on this evidence.
invalidation: trading volume normalises toward the 30-day baseline while the $40B commitment figure is reaffirmed or raised at the next quarterly report

thesis: Flagged on a 15.4% 60-day decline. Two things are true at once and this run cannot rank them. AMD's Q2 2026, reported 4 August, showed revenue up 50% with the data center segment up 107% year over year to $6.7B, and the stock fell anyway on the report; management has since guided to data center sales doubling in 2027 and server revenue up more than 80% year over year in the second half of fiscal 2026, with the MI400 launch described by CEO Lisa Su as an inflection point and an OpenAI agreement covering 6 gigawatts of Instinct GPUs starting with a 1-gigawatt rollout in the second half of 2026. Against that, the shares fell more than 4% through the $500 level on 18 August as the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index posted its steepest three-day decline since March, driven by the 30-year Treasury yield reaching 5.33% and what is described as a fundamental repricing of risk. A company-specific negative reaction to a strong print, plus a macro repricing, plus a major product cycle still ahead of launch is an unresolved mix, not a thesis.
invalidation: MI400 ships on schedule in 2026 with the initial 1-gigawatt OpenAI rollout confirmed, while long-end yields stabilise
